title: ‘It Still Really Bothers Him’: Junaid Khan on What Happens Inside the Khan Household When a Film Doesn’t Work
excerpt: Aamir Khan’s son breaks his silence on ‘Ek Din’ underperforming, Sai Pallavi feeling miscast, and navigating Bollywood with the most exacting perfectionist in the family sitting across the dinner table
body:
There is a specific kind of silence that settles over a Bollywood household when the Friday numbers come in and they are not good. Junaid Khan knows that silence well. His film *Ek Din*, produced by his father Aamir Khan’s banner and co-starring Sai Pallavi, opened to ₹1.15 crore on its first day and limped to a total of roughly ₹5 crore — a commercial failure by any measure. In a recent interview, Junaid spoke about what that felt like, and what it is like to live with a father for whom failure is not a theoretical concept but a personal affront.

“It still really bothers him,” Junaid said of Aamir Khan’s reaction to the film’s performance. “He has decades of experience and he’s been through this many times, but it doesn’t get easier. When something he’s been involved in doesn’t work, he takes it very personally.”

## The film and its problems

*Ek Din*, directed by Sunil Pandey, is a Hindi remake of the 2016 Thai romantic drama *One Day*. It tells the story of a corporate worker with transient global amnesia who lives his crush’s life for a day — a high-concept premise that, in the original, worked because of its lean runtime and emotional restraint. The Hindi adaptation, running longer and leaning into Bollywood conventions, received largely negative reviews. Critics praised Sai Pallavi’s performance but found Junaid’s screen presence underpowered and the direction pedestrian.

Sai Pallavi herself added an unexpected wrinkle when she said in an interview that she felt “miscast” in the role — a candid admission that is almost unheard of during a film’s promotional cycle. Junaid was diplomatic in response: he acknowledged her feelings without dismissing them and redirected the conversation to the broader challenges of adapting foreign material.

## The weight of the name

Being Aamir Khan’s son in Bollywood is a double-edged inheritance. The access is obvious — Junaid’s debut, *Maharaj* (2024), was a Netflix release that benefited from the Khan production machinery. But the expectations are crushing. Aamir Khan is not just a star; he is the industry’s self-appointed quality gatekeeper, the man who takes three years between films because he refuses to settle. Having that standard applied to your own nascent career, by the person who set it, is a pressure few star kids face.

Junaid addressed this directly: “I don’t want him to make a film for me. He can do one film in five years — that’s his pace, and it works for him. I need to find my own rhythm.” It is a mature statement, and it signals an awareness that the Aamir Khan brand — built on meticulous perfectionism — is both a launchpad and a cage.

## What NRI audiences see

For the Indian diaspora, Aamir Khan occupies a unique space. He is the star whose films *travel* — not just to the Gulf and Southeast Asia, where Bollywood has traditional strongholds, but to China, where *Dangal* earned over ₹1,200 crore, and to the American heartland, where *PK* played in mainstream multiplexes. NRI families treat an Aamir Khan release as an event, and they bring to it the same expectations of quality that he has spent a career cultivating.

*Ek Din* did not meet those expectations, and the NRI box-office numbers reflected it. For diaspora audiences used to paying $15–$20 for a Bollywood ticket in the US, the calculus is simple: an Aamir Khan production should justify the premium. A weak remake of a Thai film, however well-intentioned, does not.

But Junaid’s honesty about failure may ultimately be more valuable to his career than a hit would have been. The star-kid narrative in Bollywood is usually one of entitlement and denial — bad films are blamed on marketing, audiences, or release dates. Junaid’s willingness to say “it didn’t work” and to discuss his father’s disappointment openly is disarming. It suggests he understands something that many second-generation Bollywood actors do not: that audiences, especially the discerning NRI audiences who grew up on his father’s films, can smell inauthenticity.

## The road from here

Junaid has not announced his next project. *Ek Din*’s poor showing will make financiers cautious, and the protective umbrella of Aamir Khan Productions can only extend so far before the market demands that the younger Khan prove himself on his own terms. The question is not whether Junaid has talent — *Maharaj* showed he does — but whether he can find the material that unlocks it.

For Aamir Khan, the emotional investment is ongoing. He is, by all accounts, a hands-on producer who watches dailies, notes performances, and agonises over cuts. When a film fails, he does not have the luxury of distance. “It still really bothers him” is not just a quote from a son about a father — it is a portrait of a particular kind of creative anxiety that the audience rarely sees.
